opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the motivation really comes from looking at what next-token prediction is actually optimizing for. When you train with teacher forcing, the model only ever has to get the very next token right given the ground-truth prefix. That works well for a lot of things, but it pushes the model to be fairly myopic. It learns local patterns very well, but it never has to commit to some kind of global plan for where the sequence is going.

That matters a lot when you care about diversity and creativity. Think about open-ended tasks where there's a large space of valid answers, like coming up with novel connections, designing a puzzle, or generating a set of different solutions. What you really want there is for the model to sample a high-level "idea" and then execute on it coherently. With next-token prediction, all the randomness gets injected token by token at the output through temperature sampling. So you end up with this awkward trade-off. If you turn the temperature up you get diversity, but you also get incoherence, because you're randomly perturbing individual tokens rather than choosing different plans. If you keep the temperature low, you get coherent but pretty repetitive outputs, and often the model just regurgitates things it's memorized.

Multi-token prediction and diffusion-style objectives both get at this in different ways. With multi-token prediction, the model has to predict several tokens ahead, so the representation is forced to encode something about the future and not just the immediate next step. With diffusion, or teacherless training more broadly, the model generates or refines the whole sequence jointly, so it has to reason about global structure rather than greedily stitching together locally plausible pieces. In some of our experiments on minimal, controlled tasks designed to need this kind of "leap of thought," those objectives produced outputs that were both more original and less memorized than standard next-token training.

There's also a related idea we've been excited about, which is moving the randomness from the output to the input. You condition the model on a random seed or prefix and let it decode fairly deterministically from there. Somewhat surprisingly, that can match or beat temperature sampling for diversity, and it fits nicely with the view that you want to sample the plan, not the individual tokens.

I don't want to oversell it. These are early results, a lot of it is on synthetic tasks, and scaling these objectives has real engineering challenges. But I think it's a strong signal that the training objective itself, and not just the sampling procedure or post-training, shapes how creative and diverse a model can be. So it's worth seriously rethinking the next-token default.

r001.rationale: It says multi-token prediction forces the model to represent the future beyond the immediate next step, conveying that predicting multiple tokens encourages understanding broader sequence patterns.

r002.rationale: It says diffusion jointly generates or refines the sequence and encourages reasoning about global structure, but does not mention masking tokens.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, and I think the way to frame it is to start with what next-token prediction actually does to a model's representation of uncertainty.

When you train with a standard autoregressive objective, you're asking the model, at every position, to put a distribution over the very next token. And on the surface that seems fine, because the chain rule says any joint distribution factorizes that way. But in practice, the model has to commit early. If there are two very different ways a sentence or a proof or a program could unfold, and they happen to share the same first few tokens, the model is fine. But if they diverge immediately, the model is picking a branch at the first token, and once it's picked, everything downstream is conditioned on that choice. The model never had to represent "here are five genuinely different ways this could go" as a single object. It only ever had to represent the marginal over the next step.

What we found in our work on creativity, and in the follow-ups, is that this shows up as a real deficit in what I'd call diverse generation, meaning tasks where the goal isn't a single correct answer but a spread of valid, distinct outputs. Think of generating many different plausible hypotheses, or multiple distinct solutions to a combinatorial problem, or even just coming up with lots of truly different story continuations. On those tasks, next-token models tend to collapse. They become very good at producing one high-likelihood mode and then rephrasing it, and that collapse gets worse, not better, with scale and with post-training like RLHF, because those processes sharpen the distribution.

So multi-token prediction is interesting precisely because it changes what the model has to represent at a given position. If you're asked to predict the next k tokens jointly, you can't get away with a greedy local commitment. You have to hold the structure of a longer chunk in mind, and that forces the internal representation to encode global coherence rather than just the next step. In our experiments, the "teacherless" setup, where you don't feed the model its own prior predictions within the chunk, was especially effective, because it removes the crutch of conditioning on what you just said and makes the model plan.

Diffusion pushes this even further. In a discrete diffusion model, you're generating the whole sequence at once and refining it, so there's no left-to-right bottleneck at all. The model gets to look at a noisy global picture and decide what the sequence should be as a whole, which is a much more natural fit for "I want to sample from a distribution over distinct, coherent objects." And empirically, on the kinds of open-ended tasks I mentioned, diffusion models produced far more diverse outputs without sacrificing coherence, which is exactly the trade-off that's hard to get from an autoregressive model by just turning up the temperature.

I'd add one more thing, which is about the training signal itself. There's a subtle issue with next-token prediction where, when the data contains genuinely multiple valid continuations, the model is penalized for not hedging, so it learns to hedge in a way that's locally safe but globally bland. Objectives that score larger chunks give you a cleaner signal about which complete outputs are good, which I think is closer to what we actually care about.

Now, I don't want to oversell this. Autoregressive models are extraordinarily good at a lot of things, and diffusion for language still has real costs around efficiency and around how well it handles very long contexts. But I think the deeper point is that we've been treating the next-token objective as a neutral choice, and it isn't. It encodes a specific inductive bias about how to decompose uncertainty, and that bias is a bad fit for exactly the open-ended, generative, "give me many good different things" use cases that are becoming more important. So I see multi-token and diffusion objectives less as a replacement and more as a way of asking what we lose with left-to-right commitment, and whether we can get it back.

r001.rationale: The response says joint prediction of the next k tokens requires holding a longer chunk in mind and encoding global coherence, which communicates understanding the overall pattern.

r002.rationale: The response describes diffusion refining a noisy global sequence and planning the sequence as a whole, but it does not connect that planning to masking tokens in the diffusion objective.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting question is whether predicting one token at a time gives you the best learning signal for everything we want a language model to do. It’s a very powerful objective, but there are situations where several different continuations are perfectly reasonable, and the choice you make early on affects what makes sense later.

Multi-token prediction gives you a way to ask the model to learn about a longer stretch of that continuation. Diffusion offers a different way to approach this: you can refine multiple parts of a sequence together, rather than committing to each token in order. That could be useful when you want generations that are diverse but still internally consistent.

I wouldn’t say either objective automatically gives you more diversity. Autoregressive models can represent diverse distributions too. The question is whether these alternatives make it easier to learn the relationships that matter, and whether that translates into better samples for the same amount of training or inference compute. That’s why I think they’re worth exploring.

r001.rationale: It says multi-token prediction lets the model learn about a longer stretch of a continuation, where early choices affect later ones, conveying learning the broader pattern across tokens.

r002.rationale: It says diffusion can refine multiple sequence parts together, but does not state that masking tokens encourages global planning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the motivation is that there are many valid ways to continue a piece of text, and we’d like models to capture that diversity while still producing something coherent. With next-token prediction, you’re making one local prediction at a time. That’s a very powerful approach, but it raises the question of whether predicting larger pieces together could help the model capture dependencies across those choices.

Multi-token prediction is one way to explore that. Diffusion gives you another way to think about generation: you can start with an uncertain candidate and refine it, allowing different parts of the output to inform one another. That seems particularly interesting when there isn’t a single correct answer.

I wouldn’t say either objective automatically gives you better diversity. You still have to ask whether the model captures genuinely different valid possibilities, and whether those possibilities remain high quality. But they open up ways of learning and sampling that are worth investigating beyond the next-token setup.
